# MindTopo: Can Foundation Models Reason in Topological Space? Full reference for LLMs and RAG tools

Paper: "MindTopo: Can Foundation Models Reason in Topological Space?"
Authors: Yunfei Ge, Anbang Liu, Qineng Wang, Johnalbert Garnica, Jianwen Lyu, Zihan Wang, Reuben Tan, Jianfeng Gao, Ruohan Zhang, Yining Hong, Jiajun Wu, Manling Li.
Affiliations: Northwestern University, Microsoft Research, Stanford University.
Project page: https://mind-topo.github.io/
Paper: https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.11900
Code: https://github.com/mll-lab-nu/MindTopo
Dataset: https://huggingface.co/datasets/MLL-Lab/MindTopo

## What is MindTopo?

MindTopo is a benchmark of topological intuition for foundation models. It covers five topological properties (continuity, separation, order, enclosure, and knots) at two cognitive levels: reasoning over rendered scenes and planning in interactive environments. It has 13 procedurally generated task types with controllable difficulty. The primary Core Set contains 3,900 instances split evenly between an Easy and a Hard level, and the exact-input-disjoint Extended Set contains 8,780 additional instances.

## What is topological space, and why does it matter?

Spatial reasoning involves more than metric properties such as distance, angle, and shape. Topological relations remain invariant under continuous deformation: a closed rope loop can be bent, stretched, or coiled without changing its knot type. Piaget argued that topological relations precede Euclidean and projective relations in spatial development, and studies of adult vision found that the visual system extracts topological invariants before Euclidean features. Most spatial benchmarks for foundation models test metric or viewpoint-dependent relations; MindTopo targets the topological layer and asks whether models can also act on it.

## What are the five topological properties and their tasks?

- Continuity: whether a path or surface forms an unbroken whole. Reasoning tasks (2D Maze, 3D Maze): which marked points are reachable from a target point, with what-if questions about adding or removing a wall. Planning task (Pipe): rotate pipe segments by 90 degrees until every segment connects back to the source.
- Separation: the complement of proximity, the basis of object individuation. Reasoning task (Assembly): given an assembled object and candidate sub-assemblies, select the topologically separable component. Planning task (One Stroke): draw a single path through a colored grid that keeps same-colored cells together and separates different colors.
- Order: the sequential arrangement of elements along a path. Reasoning tasks (Bead, Origami Point): list bead colors along a twisted string from a starting bead, or track marked points through a sequence of folds. Planning task (Swap): reach a target color permutation by moving blocks into a single empty slot.
- Enclosure: the inside/outside relation induced by a closed boundary. Reasoning tasks (Sheep, Hole): which animals lie strictly inside a fence, and how many through-holes a solid has. Planning task (Chat Noir): place one block per turn on a hexagonal grid to trap a cat before it reaches the edge.
- Knots: entanglement that persists under deformation, the "mother structure" coordinating other topological relations. Reasoning task (Knots): is a loop truly knotted or only tangled, are two loops linked, which rings become free after one is cut. Planning task (Untangle): move rope ends on a peg grid until no two ropes cross.

## What are the two cognitive levels?

- Reasoning: an instance is a rendered observation, a question, and a reference answer computed from the scene state. Scalar and categorical answers are scored by exact match; unordered answers are compared as sets.
- Planning: a foundation model acts as a closed-loop agent. At each step it receives a rendered observation and selects an action; the simulator updates the state. An episode succeeds only if the goal predicate is satisfied within the step budget.

A model may recognize that a loop is knotted yet fail to plan how to untangle it; the two levels test whether reasoning about a relation transfers to action.

## How is the data built?

A fully automated four-stage pipeline with fixed seeds: scene generation (task-specific simulators or rendering scripts), topological annotation (reference answers and success conditions computed programmatically from the scene state), difficulty control (parameters such as wall count, grid size, and crossing count produce Easy and Hard levels), and instance generation (templated reasoning questions or planning episodes). Task-specific acceptance checks reject invalid, ambiguous, or unsolvable instances. Text-only, answer-prior, appearance-only, and symbolic-input controls test for shortcuts.

## How large is the benchmark?

The Core Set has 3,900 evaluation instances: each of the 13 tasks contributes 300 (150 Easy, 150 Hard), giving 2,400 reasoning questions over 8 tasks and 1,500 planning episodes over 5 tasks. The Extended Set adds 8,780 instances with no exact-input overlap with Core.

## How do current models perform?

13 hosted MLLMs were evaluated with deterministic decoding: GPT-6 Astra, GPT-5.6-Sol, GPT-5.5, GPT-5.4-mini, Gemini-3.1-Flash-Lite, Gemini-3.1-Pro, Claude-Haiku-5.5 (proprietary); Nemotron-Nano-12B-VL-v2, Qwen3.5-397B-A17B, Llama-4-Maverick-17B-128E, Ministral-3-14B-Instruct-2512, InternVL3.5-241B, Gemma-4-31B-IT (open-weight).

- Every model scores lower on planning than on reasoning. GPT-6 Astra leads both: 59.54% reasoning, 49.80% planning.
- The gap widens below the frontier: Claude-Haiku-5.5 drops from 19.87% to 5.40%, Gemini-3.1-Pro from 19.17% to 4.20%.
- No hosted open-weight model exceeds 1% average planning success, close to the 0.53% of a random legal policy.
- Untangle is the hardest planning environment (best 20.67%); Swap is the most accessible below the frontier.
- Humans (five professional annotators, Easy level, inter-annotator agreement 0.89) reach 94.23% on reasoning and 99.87% on planning; GPT-6 Astra reaches 76.33% and 81.87%. It matches humans on 2D Maze, Pipe, and Swap but trails far behind on Untangle, Bead, Sheep, and Hole.

## Does training help?

Qwen3-VL-2B-Instruct was trained on the Easy level with supervised fine-tuning (SFT), GRPO reinforcement learning (RL), and SFT followed by RL. SFT followed by RL lifts average reasoning accuracy from 14.24% to 51.53% (Knots 11.20% to 79.60%, Sheep 9.40% to 58.20%), but average planning success only from 0.20% to 6.33%; Pipe stays at 0%. 2D Maze, which needs connectivity across the whole scene, barely improves. Leave-one-task-out RL transfers to held-out tasks only in selected cases.

## Where do models fail?

910 failures of Gemini-3.1-Pro and InternVL3.5-241B were labeled with a seven-class taxonomy in causal order. Reasoning failures concentrate in perception grounding (47.5%) and instruction following (33.8%). In planning, feature-state prediction, dynamic violations, and action planning together account for 50.9% of failures. The dominant planning failure depends strongly on the environment.

## Can image or video generation act as a world model?

With GPT-5.6-Luna as planner, rendering the predicted next state with GPT-Image-2 raises success to 68.57% on Sheep and 61.90% on 2D Maze but gives 0% on One Stroke: generated frames keep local cues but not invariants that span a trajectory. An automatic verifier checked 1,890 video rollouts from six video generators (LTX-2.3, LTX-2.5, Veo-3.1-Lite, Wan2.2-I2V-A14B, MiniMax-H3, Seedance-2.5) on One Stroke, Pipe, and Untangle. Up to 35.2% of rollouts end in a solved final frame, yet the process-valid rate is 0.0% for every generator on every task. A manual audit of 119 Wan2.2-I2V-A14B rollouts found dynamics violations in 116, topological-invariance errors in 93, and consistency errors in 90.

## Key numbers at a glance

- 5 topological properties; 2 cognitive levels; 13 task types; 3,900 Core instances (2,400 reasoning, 1,500 planning; 150 Easy + 150 Hard per task); 8,780 exact-input-disjoint Extended instances.
- 13 MLLMs evaluated; 7 video generative models studied.
- Best model (GPT-6 Astra): 59.54% reasoning, 49.80% planning. Easy level: 76.33% / 81.87% vs. human 94.23% / 99.87%.
- Video rollouts: up to 35.2% solved final frames, 0 of 1,890 process-valid.

## Contributions

1. Formulating topological intuition as an evaluation target for spatial reasoning, grounding five properties in cognitive science and formal topology.
2. A scalable benchmark of 13 procedurally generated task types probing these properties through reasoning and planning under controllable difficulty.
3. A benchmark of 13 MLLMs and agent configurations involving seven video generative models, revealing a consistent gap between reasoning about topological structure and acting on it.
4. A study of SFT and RL on Qwen3-VL-2B-Instruct, showing that training improves reasoning more than planning and produces uneven gains on held-out tasks.
